title: Blessing on seeing people
hookLine: blessings exist for seeing a great scholar, a ruler, or a friend not seen in a year
last: THE WORLD HAS BLESSINGS BUILT IN.

lines: A YEAR SINCE THEY LAST MET.
cards: The arrivals hall at an airport, late afternoon. The doors slide open, and someone comes through pulling a suitcase, looking around. Across the rope, someone else spots them and lights up.
They haven't seen each other in a year, maybe longer. A shout, a run, a hug that nearly knocks the suitcase over. It doesn't look like a religious moment.
The Talmud has a blessing for it anyway, and its words are startling. Today: mechayeh hametim.

teach.b: The Talmud lists blessings for seeing people, the way it lists blessings for seeing the sea. For a great Torah scholar, you bless God, who has shared of his wisdom with those who revere him.

For a great scholar who isn't Jewish, there's a blessing too: who has given of his wisdom to flesh and blood. So the rabbis built into daily life a blessing for learning wherever it shows up, in anyone.

There are matching blessings on seeing a king or a ruler: who has shared of his glory, and who has given of his glory to flesh and blood. You bless not the person, but the source of what you see in them. Now the friend.
Seeing a close friend after thirty days, you say Shehecheyanu, the blessing for firsts: who kept us alive and brought us to this time.
After more than twelve months, the Talmud says something bigger: blessed is the one who revives the dead. Mechayeh hametim, the same phrase from the daily prayer about God's power to give life back.
The rabbis aren't saying the friend was dead. The Talmud gives its own reason for the twelve months: the dead are forgotten from the heart only after a year.
So after a year apart, it treats a reunion like being given someone back. A hug in an airport can be a blessing, and so can a Shabbat dinner, or walking into the room where an old friend is waiting.

how: Jews say special blessings on seeing an outstanding Torah scholar, a great scholar of any people, or a head of state, and on seeing a close friend after thirty days (Shehecheyanu) or after twelve months (mechayeh hametim).

games.q: who gets which blessing — tap the pairs.
p: given of his wisdom to flesh and blood

s: the Talmud has a blessing for seeing a non-Jewish scholar
who has given of his wisdom to flesh and blood.
the blessing on seeing a ruler praises the ruler
it blesses God, the source of the glory you see in them.
after a year apart, you bless the one who revives the dead
mechayeh hametim: a reunion feels like being given someone back.

games.q: you walk into a room and see a friend you haven't seen in over a year. what blessing does the Talmud give?
games.why: mechayeh hametim, who revives the dead: after a year, seeing a friend is like being given them back.

practice: Let a face come to mind, someone you haven't seen or spoken to in a long time; picture them laughing, and remember one thing you love about them. Now picture seeing them again: the doorway, the hug, what you'd say first.
If you pray, you can bless the one who gave you this person.

wordCard.voice: Mechayeh hametim. Who revives the dead: the blessing said on seeing a friend after a year apart, as if given back to you.

orig.note: Hebrew: who revives the dead. the same words appear in the daily standing prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: seeing you is a blessing. Wisdom, glory and old friends all have their words. That's day one hundred eighteen.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58b (a friend after thirty days, after twelve months)
